sentences.text: Minotaurasaurus ramachandrani is the only known species of this extinct genus, a thyreophoran ankylosaurid dinosaur.

The type specimen is a virtually complete and intact skull measuring 30 centimetres in length and 43 centimetres in width, featuring large, ornate nasal osteoderms that give it a bull-like appearance with laterally open nostril windows.

The skull roof displays an unfused occiput, pyramid-shaped caputegulae covering most of the surface except near the orbits, and highly sculptured squamosal horns that are narrow, cylindrical, and more slender and tapering than those of other ankylosaurids.
In dorsal view, the skull is triangular and features large, ornate nasal osteoderms that give it a bull-like appearance with laterally open nostril windows.
The initial estimate of 4.2 meters likely underestimates the adult size because the known specimen is immature.
A second specimen shows insect burrows in a pattern unique to Late Cretaceous Gobi deposits.
The genus Minotaurasaurus and the species Minotaurasaurus ramachandrani were named and described in 2009 by Clifford Miles and Clark Miles.
The type specimen skull was purchased in 2003 for $10,000 by neuroscientist Vilayanur S. Ramachandran at a showcase in Arizona before being formally described and named in 2009.

Fossil remains of Minotaurasaurus were recovered from the Ukhaa Tolgod locality in the Djadochta Formation within the Gobi Desert, though it is not specified whether the location is in China or Mongolia.
Minotaurasaurus was a herbivorous bulk feeder with a broad, sub-rectangular muzzle.
Researchers suggest Minotaurasaurus may have relied on hindgut fermentation or eaten succulent plants rather than complex chewing due to its dry environment.
Park et al. (2021) suggested a shift from bulk to selective feeding in Mongolian ankylosaurines was caused by climate change or competition with hadrosaurids.
Minotaurasaurus likely had a tail club used for defense and was covered in protective osteoderms.

Minotaurasaurus ramachandrani exhibits typical characteristics of many Upper Cretaceous ankylosaurids, though the characteristics of the cranial box are more primitive than those of other ankylosaurids from the Gobi Desert.
The parent group of Minotaurasaurus is Ankylosaurinae, and it belongs to the family Ankylosauridae.
Thomas et al. (2012) and Han et al. (2014) recovered Minotaurasaurus as the sister taxon to Pinacosaurus grangeri in phylogenetic analyses.
Minotaurasaurus lived during the late Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 75 to 71 million years ago, in what is now Asia.
It lived in an arid environment with sand dunes and short-lived water bodies during a warm, semiarid climate.

The holotype specimen has been suspected to have been illegally exported from Mongolia, a point that led to criticism from paleontologists regarding the questionable legal origins of the specimen during the original description.

Arbour et al. (2014) and Arbour & Currie (2015) considered Minotaurasaurus a junior synonym of Tarchia kielanae based on a shared furrow near the squamosal horn, a conclusion reached in a 2014 study by Victoria Arbour, Philip Currie, and Demchig Badamgarav.

However, Penkalski & Tumanova (2016) argued that Minotaurasaurus is a valid taxon distinct from Tarchia due to differences in squamosal horns and caputegulae, a view supported by a 2016 redescription of Tarchia cranial anatomy which concluded that Minotaurasaurus is a distinct taxon.
